children: Crude oil futures fell for a second straight session Thursday as concerns eased over Middle East supply disruptions, with Saudi Arabia aiming to ship crude through the Strait of Hormuz as it shifts crude loadings away from the out-of-service Yanbu port and possibly restoring some oil flows soon through its damaged East-West pipeline.

With Saudi's export options no longer feasible, at least for now, a shuttle service that slips oil through the Strait of Hormuz, along with the kingdom's track record of fixing damaged infrastructure quickly, now looks like the best hope to cool oil prices,
The Wall Street Journal
reported.

The United Arab Emirates' state-owned ADNOC oil company has been using its own vessels and hiring ships to take crude out through the strait; oil tankers leave Hormuz in a convoy under U.S. military protection, and the oil is then unloaded onto another vessel waiting in the Gulf of Oman by a ship-to-ship transfer.

Estimates of how much oil is getting out of the strait vary widely since activity is difficult to track as ships turn off their transponders, but commodities traders think ~9M barrels of oil and refined products may be slipping out daily,
WSJ
said.
Saudi Aramco (

) has a knack for fixing damaged infrastructure quickly, which could also help to get oil flowing again, as it has the Middle East's deepest supply chain and the best ability to repair assets, especially pipelines, IEA oil analyst Rebecca Schulz told
WSJ

The ramp-up in attacks on Saudi Arabia shows the vulnerability of the country's energy infrastructure, but the Saudi government's reliance on oil for 55% of its revenues means the incentive to get crude flowing again is high.

Rising crude prices have pulled back following reports that Saudi Arabia was offering more ​crude cargoes through ship-to-ship transfers offshore Oman outside the Strait of Hormuz and was seeking to return about half the capacity of its East-West oil pipeline within days.

President Trump told Axios he was approaching a "big decision" on whether to re-escalate attacks on Iran, with a meeting with Persian Gulf leaders planned for next week in New York, and China reportedly has asked Iran to rein in Houthi militants after an appeal to China by the Saudis.

Diplomatic signals are providing some relief to fears of broader escalation, although the physical market remains tight, limiting scope for further price declines, Exness senior market strategist Christopher Tahir said in a note.

"Tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz continues to fall, while tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis leave Red Sea shipping and regional energy infrastructure exposed to renewed disruption," Tahir wrote.
Front-month Nymex crude
for October slipped 0.5% to $101.91/bbl, and front-month Brent crude
for November delivery dropped 0.9% to $104.82/bbl, two days after both benchmarks settled at their highest levels since May 19.
U.S. natural gas futures

finished little changed, with some support from a below-average weekly storage build that trimmed the inventory surplus over the five-year average to 118 Bcf from 148 Bcf; the Nymex front-month October contract rose 0.3% to $2.901/MMBtu.

title: Crude oil posts back-to-back losses as Saudi supply outlook improves
